Prices are TCGplayer's market price as Scryfall publishes it each night, near mint. Table 1 starts keeping a card's daily prices once anyone wants it, so a card you've just added shows its trend after a day, and its alerts after a week. Individual TCGplayer listings aren't read.
Collection → Import. Bring a whole collection over from another app as one change you can undo, or take it out again.
CSV exports from ManaBox, Moxfield, Archidekt, Deckbox, Dragon Shield, TCGplayer and Delver Lens, telling the format apart by its header. Any other CSV with a name column works too.
Each line matches by Scryfall id, then set and collector number, then set and name, then name (the original printing). Condition and language carry over, on each app's own grading scale.
before anything is written: matched cards and printings, unmatched lines (each with Fix or Skip), and the total value.
or Replace collection (asks first and says how many cards that removes). Large files go in parts; a failure partway can be retried without doubling anything. One Undo takes it all back.
ManaBox binders and wishlists, Dragon Shield folders, and Moxfield/Deckbox tradelist counts (into a for-trade "Trade binder").
for Moxfield or ManaBox, with binder and tradelist columns. Both read back to the same collection.
Point the camera at a card, or a stack you flip through. Recognition happens on the phone against the downloaded card file: no photo leaves the device and nothing waits on the network.

The camera reads only the card inside the outline on screen: of the cards it can see, the one nearest the outline's center, so cards lying around it are ignored. It reads that card's text and matches the name to the catalog, handling double-faced cards, names cut off at the edge, and a misread letter or so. Tokens and art cards aren't scanned.

entries.t: Split cards, and cards held turned
entries.x: when most of the text in view reads sideways (a split card held upright) or upside down, the scanner reads the lines in the text's own direction, title first. Every half of a split card (Fire // Ice, fuse and Aftermath cards, Rooms) names it: the first half as before, a later half (Ice, Memory) when it's read whole and no other card has that name, and any two halves read anywhere on the card. Upright cards read as before.

The set code and collector number at the bottom pick the printing (the copyright year and prerelease date stamps help); otherwise the original printing. A card with no readable English name can match by set and number alone.

Alpha, Beta, Unlimited and Revised print no set, number or year, so the scanner guesses the most printed, Revised (then Unlimited, Beta, Alpha), and a foreign one its Foreign Black Border printing. An artist line with no copyright year tells it the card is from 1993–94 (4th Edition on prints a year).

when nothing printed names the set, the scanner reads the card's border color from the camera picture (a few brightness points around the card; on Android along the outline). Black goes in as Beta, white as Revised, a French name with a black border as Foreign Black Border. A border it can't tell (dim light, a sleeve) falls back to Revised, and your fix still sets the next guess.

entries.t: Your fix is the next guess
entries.x: change a scanned card's printing and the next card the scanner can't tell apart goes in as that set, nearest that collector number. Fix one Beta card and a Beta stack follows; fix one retro fetchland and the rest come in retro. Anything the camera does read still wins.

the card file carries each printing's illustrator and frame. An "Illus." credit means a 1993 or 1997 frame, old cards and retro-frame reprints alike, so a retro Misty Rainforest goes in as MH2's even when only its name, rules and credit were read; an artist after a brush means a 2003-or-newer frame; and the artist's name read (a letter or two off is fine) tells variants of one set apart. The number at the end of a copyright line ("© 2024 Wizards of the Coast 407"), lone numbers on cards without power and toughness, and more spellings of the set code count too, and what the last frames of the same card read is remembered, so a set code in one frame and the number in another pick the printing together. What no text tells is left: The List reprints, prerelease stamps the camera can't read, Unlimited from Revised.

A card counts once its name holds steady: 0.2 s when two frames read the same exact printing, 0.4 s when one did, 0.8 s without (and read at least three times). A second of misreads doesn't start it over. It can't count again until it has left the frame for a second, so holding it still never adds two.
a card's name is only ever taken from above its type line, so a name in the flavor text never names the card.
while the camera is scanning, so a long stack never locks the phone halfway. Changing a row's printing or language, or closing the scanner, lets it dim again.
Cards in German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Japanese, Korean and Chinese match by their printed name. Nobody picks a language.

entries.t: The copy goes in as the language the card says.
entries.x: A language code next to the set code ("WAR • JP") decides it; otherwise the language of the name the camera read, so a card read by its German name goes in as German. An English name doesn't say, since many cards print the English name in every language, so those go in as the language you add new copies in. When a name reads the same in two languages (often Spanish and Portuguese once accents are dropped), your new-copies language wins if it's one of the two.

The camera reads Latin and Cyrillic first. When the text in view names no card for 0.6 s it switches to reading Chinese, Japanese and Korean, stays there while cards match, and switches back after 1.2 s of misses.

Japanese, Chinese and Korean are three readers, one a frame in turn. The reader that names a card stays; a frame read before a switch counts for the reader that read it; every reader gets a frame before it goes back to Latin; and the next switch starts with the reader that named the last card. The three language models come from Google Play services: the app asks for them at install and again when the scanner opens if they're missing (until they arrive those scripts can't be read).

the camera at the top of the Collection tab scans a pile, then Add opens Add to over the scanner for every card at once: Collection, Deck (then its section), Cube, Binder, Want (any printing, these printings, or these printings and finishes; one want per card) or Trade (new or open; Get, or Give when you own every card). The camera takes nothing while the list is open, and closing it goes back to scanning with the cards kept. A pick adds everything in one go, each card as its row shows it (printing, finish, condition, language), closes the scanner, and the Collection tab says what went where, with Undo for the collection, a binder, a deck or a cube.

every scanner shows each card's price on its own line under the row: one copy in its finish and condition ("$9.00"; "≈ $7,992.55" when it's Cardmarket's converted; "No price" when there's none), and the bar adds the total ("12 scanned · $83.40"). Prices load in the background, so with no signal the rows just have no price line.
everything scanned goes in as one batch when you tap Done, and one Undo takes it all back. The cards show in your collection (and binder) straight away, without waiting for the server.
(Add, remove or replace): scanned cards go into the section you picked as one edit, in the printing and finish the scanner read.
scanned cards go in new, straight into the binder. Wants: each scanned card becomes a want.
cards you give match only cards (and printings) you own, preferring copies in a for-trade binder; cards you get match any card.
piles after a set draft.
Each scanned row shows its language (the one the card says, else the one you add new copies in); tap it to change it. When you give cards in a trade, the scan keeps the language of the copy you own.
The camera can't tell foil, so each scanned row has a finish toggle. Tap a row to change its printing; rows marked "Check printing" are the ones it wasn't sure of.

with cards scanned, the back arrow (or Android's Back) asks "Add the N cards you scanned?" with Add N, Leave without adding and Keep scanning; no card is taken while it asks. With nothing scanned it just closes.

Nobody is asked to report a bad scan; what people already do says it. Changing a scanned row's printing, deleting a row and adding the right card by hand, or adding a card by hand after the scanner couldn't read it (backing out with nothing taken, or a couple of seconds of a card it couldn't name since the last one it took) each send a small report: the text the camera read (never an image), what it picked and what the right card was. Reports go in the background and can be turned off in Account → Settings → Improve scanning.
A trade is your record of a swap: the cards you give and the cards you get, side by side in two columns. Confirming it updates your collection.

Add cards to either side by search or by scanning. What you give comes from your own copies, for-trade binders first (the binder is named); what you get can be any card and printing, and can go straight into a binder.

Each line keeps its printing, finish, condition and language; a card you get can be set to another condition or language from its menu. Each side shows its total value from market prices, each card priced in its condition. Gets that meet a want or a Missing line are marked, with "over your max" when the price is above your limit.
Name the other person and add a note if you like, or start the trade from a trade match. Drafts save as you edit; you can keep up to 50 open.

applies the whole trade to your collection as one change: given copies come off, received copies go on, and the wants they meet come off your list. If you no longer own something you're giving, nothing changes. Undo reverses the whole trade.

The Trades screen lists your trade matches first (each person, what they have that you want and what they want of yours, and the value; with none, a row explains how matches start), then drafts, then confirmed trades as your history. Trade history is always private.

Decks and cubes don't reserve copies. Before confirming, the app checks every card you're giving: if a deck or cube would need more copies than you'll have left, it names them and asks whether to remove them from the lists (sideboard first, then main) or keep them listed (they then show as missing). Considering cards don't count. Cancel keeps the draft.
Decks have Main deck, Sideboard and Considering, and Commander and Oathbreaker decks a command zone. Cubes have Main and Considering. Considering is ideas: it never counts as missing.

Decks start grouped by type (creatures, instants, lands…), cubes by color; View → Group by switches either to type, color, color identity (each color combination, Azorius to Five-color) or mana value (0 to 7+, then lands). Inside each group, cards go by name, or by mana value or set from View → Sort. The grid and stacks keep the same groups, and the sideboard shows its own cards.

Each line says what you own and what's missing, and the Decks list shows the total. Any copy of the card covers a line: any printing, finish or language. Copies of the printing and finish the line names count first, then your other copies of that card, line by line; one copy covers one line. "Owned N" on a row counts the card in any printing; a printing's own row, opened under a card with several, counts that printing. Basic lands are never missing: their lines just say how many you own, and in Grid and Stacks they never get the red short mark.
name it, pick a format, then add cards. Or import a list, or (decks) find one online.

pick Commander or Oathbreaker for a new deck and choose its command zone right there. A Commander deck takes a commander (a legendary creature or planeswalker) and, if it can have one, a partner or background. An Oathbreaker deck takes an oathbreaker (a planeswalker) and a signature spell (an instant or sorcery). Each goes in as the card's original printing. On the deck's screen, Command zone sits above the cards in every view, as two cards side by side (commander and partner, or oathbreaker and signature spell): tap a card for Open card, Change or Remove, or an empty slot to choose one. A change is one edit in the version history. An imported deck's commander shows there too. Oathbreaker is new as a format; Table 1 doesn't check Oathbreaker legality yet.
a deck's or cube's Edit has a Name row; Change renames it (trimmed, up to 60 characters). The new name shows everywhere at once and the lists re-sort.
a deck's or cube's Edit has a Format row; pick another format and the deck keeps its cards. Switching a deck to Commander or Oathbreaker brings up its command zone to fill.

choosing a commander (or partner, oathbreaker or signature spell) from the deck's screen lists the deck's own cards that fit first, then every card. Tapping one of the deck's own moves that copy in, out of the main deck or sideboard; replacing a commander sends the old one back to the main deck. In Commander and Oathbreaker decks, Edit's Move to and a card's Section offer the command zone too.

the partner slot appears only when the commander can have one (Partner, Partner with, a partner group such as Partner—Father & son, Friends forever, Choose a Background, Doctor's companion, or a Time Lord Doctor), and its search offers only cards that pair: another card with partner (or the same group, or Friends forever), the card named by Partner with (the search opens on it), a Background, the Doctor, or a Doctor's companion. The empty slot says which.
sits at the top of every deck, cube and binder: Private, Friends or Anyone. New decks start Private, so a brew never leaks.

works like Cube Cobra's: an Add box (the catalog, Scryfall syntax, or Scan) and a Remove or replace box (only the list's own cards) on one screen. Pick a card in either. With only a card to remove, the button removes one copy; with both picked it reads Replace and swaps that copy for the new card in the same section, as one edit. The + on a search result adds a card at once.

a card with several printings or finishes in a section is one row (total, "3 printings", what's missing) with a chevron that opens each line; View → Expand all printings opens them all. Edit mode always shows every line.
inside the list hides sections with no match; stats, Missing and legality still count the whole list.
mode: steppers on every line; tap a line to move it between sections, remove it, or change its printing or finish.
on the printing screen choose how many copies to change, then the printing and finish. Moving 2 of 4 to foil leaves 2 non-foil and 2 foil as separate lines.

each line has a language as well as a printing and finish, so 3 English and 1 Japanese copy of a card are two lines. Lines in another language show it ("JA") in the list, edit mode and version history. Cards added from search start in English unless the printing exists only in another language; a card added from your collection keeps its language; scanned cards go in as the language they were read as. Changing a line's printing keeps its language, unless the new printing has its own. Missing counts your copies in any language. Exports and shared links don't carry the language yet.

each line also has a condition (NM, LP, MP, HP, DMG), so 2 near-mint and 1 lightly played copy are two lines. A copy added from your collection or a binder keeps its condition, and scanned cards take the one picked in the scanner; anything else starts near mint. Rows, edit mode, version history and Change printing show it when it isn't near mint ("LP"). Nothing on the deck picks it: the card's page from a deck shows no Condition. Changing the printing, Match collection, moving sections and Sync with Cube Cobra keep it. Exports and shared links don't carry it yet.
a deck or cube from Edit mode; the copy starts its own history. Delete removes it from every device.
the current version (see Importing and exporting lists), or make a deck image.
under Add to collection, "12 to buy · $83.40" opens the Buy screen: skip what you own, exact printings or one cart, tokens and boards, the total, then TCGplayer.
A plan for each matchup: what comes in, what goes out, and notes. Sideboard guide sits under Stats on every deck except Commander and Oathbreaker ("3 matchups · sideboard 15").

+ adds one, picked from the format's Insights archetypes by share (when Insights covers the format) or typed (up to 40 characters). Each row reads "IN 3 · OUT 3" or "NO CHANGES", with Check when something's off. A matchup's Edit renames it, moves it up or down, or deletes it. Up to 40 matchups.

a matchup opens on two cells, In and Out, and its plan below them ("+2 Fury", "−1 Ragavan"). In lists your sideboard, then Considering, each with − and + up to the copies in the deck; Out lists the main deck. Cards stay in the order you added them. Ins needn't match outs: the rules let you change the deck's size as long as it stays legal.

the In screen's search adds any card to Considering and brings one in, so you can try more than 15 cards while you work the guide out. The Sideboard screen lists Sideboard and Considering with "In 4 matchups" on each card; tap one to move a copy (or all) to the other section.

a card no longer in the deck, more copies than you have, copies coming from Considering ("not printed until it's in the sideboard"), and the deck going under 60 cards after sideboarding (100 for Canadian Highlander; Other isn't checked). The guide screen also says when the sideboard is over 15 in a Constructed format.
per matchup, up to 1,000 characters: play or draw, what to watch for, what to keep.

the print icon opens the page as it will print, then Print (the phone's print sheet, or the browser's). White paper in Table 1's mono type with uppercase labels and thin boxes, the teal only as the line under the header; matchups in two columns, each box kept whole, then your sideboard. Only what you can bring in at a tournament is printed: cards still in Considering, and cards no longer in the deck, are left off and counted above the preview. Under the header: "MTR 2.11 · Between games only · Remove from the play area before each game" (the rules allow brief notes made before the match, read between games). It warns past two pages ("a sheet or two") and when the sideboard has more than 15 cards. A guide on your phone is fine at Regular REL; at Competitive REL bring it printed.
The guide saves with the deck, syncs to your devices and works offline. Only you see it: shared decks and links don't include it.
Under Stats, each of your decks in an Insights format (Standard, Pioneer, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Pauper, Canadian Highlander) shows the archetype it plays as, by the same rules Insights uses.

with its win rate over the last 30 days ("Win 53.3%": matches against other archetypes in every event Insights reads, draws counting as not won; shown from 20 matches) and its change on last week ("▲ 2.1 pts on last week": this week's win rate against the week before's, when both have 20 matches; "Same as last week" when flat).
and Bad against: its three best and three worst matchups over 90 days, one a line ("Boros Energy 58%"), each from at least 20 decided matches.

the archetype row reads "88% similar" on its own line above the win rate: the deck against the archetype's 10 closest lists of the last 90 days (the year when there are none), each the share of copies the two have in common out of the larger deck, basic lands and the sideboard left out, averaged over the ten. A deck copied from a recent list reads 100%.
a deck Spice calls a Brew (50 or more) shows no In the meta rows; the archetype's numbers say little about a deck that plays mostly other cards.

Tap any of the rows to open the archetype's Insights page over the deck; Back returns to the deck. A deck no archetype rule names reads "In the meta · Doesn't match an archetype Insights knows"; decks in other formats, and roto decks, show nothing.
Built a deck or cube you now own in paper? Add to collection on its screen says how many copies of its exact printings you're missing and opens a screen to add them.

adds only what your collection lacks of the exact printing, finish and language the list names: a copy you own in another printing, finish or language doesn't count here, so a deck listing a Japanese foil Ragavan adds one even if you own an English one (basic lands are never missing, so it leaves them out). That differs on purpose from the deck's own "missing", which counts any copy of the card; Every card adds every copy the list holds, basics included, for when you've bought or opened another set of it.
Each card goes in as the printing, finish, language and condition the list records. A deck's Sideboard switch decides whether its sideboard comes too; Considering is never added.

There's no condition or language to pick: each copy goes in as the condition its line records (near mint unless it came from your collection or a scan with another condition) and the line's language. With Missing, copies you own in any condition count, those in the line's own condition first. The screen lists every card it will add with its count and language.
It all goes in as one change: Undo takes it back out.

a card opened from a deck or cube has Add to collection in its details (the list icon): add the copies you're missing of the listed printings (by the same exact rule, in each line's condition and language), every copy the list holds, or one copy of a listed printing. A basic land never has copies missing, so its row reads "Basic land · add the copies listed here" and offers every copy or one.
Roto decks don't offer it: their cards belong to the cube.

A cube you keep on Cube Cobra too can be brought up to date from there. Sync with Cube Cobra sits on every cube of your own (not roto decks), under Export, and says which Cube Cobra cube it follows ("cubecobra.com · lindmark").
a cube imported from a Cube Cobra link remembers it. Change link points it at another cube.

a summary ("2 in · 2 out · 1 new printing", or "Up to date"), then In (on Cube Cobra, not in your cube), Out (in your cube, not on Cube Cobra) and New printing or finish (the same card in another printing or finish: "2ED #266 → LEA #265", "Non-foil → Foil"). Main and Considering are compared on their own: a card moved from one to the other is Out of one and In the other. Tap a card for its page. Cards Cube Cobra lists that aren't in the card data are named and left out, as on import.
stay as you set them: Cube Cobra doesn't record languages, so a Japanese Mana Drain that Cube Cobra still lists stays Japanese. A new printing that exists only in one language takes that language.
saves the whole cube as one new version, "Synced with Cube Cobra"; Restore in Version history puts the old one back. Keep as it is goes back without changing anything.
If the cube changed on another device between checking and accepting, nothing is saved: it says so and offers Check again.
Every change is kept. Edits within 10 minutes of each other become one version, so a run of +1s is one entry.
Open any version to see what was added and removed; Restore makes it current again as a new version. Nothing is ever overwritten.
The few cards that stand for a deck, a cube, a binder or your whole collection, picked by you.

On a card's page, under the list icon, Make it a hero makes it a hero of where you opened it from: that deck or cube, that binder, or (from anywhere else) your collection. Tap again to stop. A deck's Edit mode offers it on each line too.
Up to 10 per place. A hero is the card, not a printing, so changing a printing keeps it; the art shown is the printing that deck or binder holds.
up to three hero cards fan out next to the name in Decks, Cubes and Binders, and on the Collection home's All cards row.
a hero's row is a shade lighter with a white edge; in the grid and stacks it gets a white outline.
Deleting a deck, cube or binder drops its heroes. Heroes are private like the rest of your Library.
Heroes save to your account and follow you to every device, on iPhone, Android and the web.
Every Add cards search (collection, decks and cubes, binders, wants) takes Scryfall's search syntax. Adv opens a form that writes it for you.
Card name, card text, type line, colors (exactly, including or at most), mana value, rarity, set code and the format it's legal in. Search puts the syntax in the box, so you can tweak it there.

Name, type (t:dragon), colors (c:r, c=wu, c:izzet), mana value (mv<=3), mana cost, rarity, set, collector number, year, language, foil, format legality (f:modern, banned:), mana produced, with -, or and parentheses. Instant, from the card file on your phone.
Anything else, such as card text (o:"draw a card"), power or color identity, is asked of Scryfall once you stop typing, and shows "from Scryfall". It needs a connection.
A plain name is the usual name search. When a search names a set, rarity or year, the result shows (and adds) that printing.

A Stats row under each deck ("24 lands · avg MV 1.72 · $1,535.36") or cube ("W 44 · U 56 · …") opens the numbers. Everything is worked out on your device from the card file, so it's instant and offline.
by mana value, creatures against other spells; types; average mana value with and without lands.
colored symbols in the costs next to the lands, dorks and rocks that make each color (fetch lands count for the colors they find).
per format with reasons, including copy limits.
at market for each printing and finish, leaving out basic lands (your collection's value still counts the basics you own), and the tokens the deck makes.
with London mulligans: draw seven, mulligan, put cards on the bottom, keep drawing.
the chance of seeing at least k of a card or card type by each turn, on the play or the draw.
, curve per color and type mix.
expected copies per pack by color, type or mana value, for a pack size you set.
drawn from the cube.

How far a deck or cube strays from the ones like it, from 0 to 100. Each non-basic card in the main deck (and the command zone) counts by its copies. A card played in a quarter or more of the similar lists is stock and adds nothing. A rarer card adds more, up to its full weight for a card never seen. Basic lands never count, and sideboard cards are listed but not scored.
Stock 0–9 (nine in ten tournament lists), Tuned 10–24, Spicy 25–49, Brew 50 and up.

are the tournament lists Insights reads, never older than a year. First the deck's own archetype, named by the same rules as Insights: its lists from the last 90 days, or the year if that's under 30 lists. A deck that comes out as Other, or whose archetype has too few lists, is compared with the archetype that plays the most of its cards. If even that one plays under a quarter of them, it's compared with the whole format, and Spice says "Nothing close in Modern". A deck copied from an Insights list isn't compared with that list.
decks are one-ofs that share few cards, so each card is compared with the year's lists that could play it (their colors include the card's), and a card counts as stock from a tenth of them.

the Stats row ends with "Spice 34". Stats opens on the score and word in teal, then what it was compared with ("412 Boros Energy lists · last 90 days · MTGO and TopDeck.gg"). Under that come Spiciest cards ("4 Ancient Grudge · in 2 of 412 lists", "never seen"; the first eight, then Show all) and Stock cards you don't play (cards in half the similar lists or more, up to 12; none when the comparison is the whole format). Tap a card for its page. A deck or cube shared with you, on a profile or through a link, has a Spice row that opens the same.
(Commander, Premodern and the rest) say "No tournament lists for this format yet".

are to be compared with the 20 most similar of Cube Cobra's popular public cubes, each counted by how alike it is, with the nearest named ("LSVCube · 62% alike"). Cube Cobra's terms don't allow reading its cubes without permission, so Table 1 is asking first. Until then a cube's Spice says "No cubes to compare with yet".
Worked out on the server, at most once a day for each version of a deck. Anyone who can see the deck or cube can see its Spice.
A deck as one picture, laid out the way tournament sites show decklists, to post or send. On every deck (yours, or one a friend shares) tap Deck image.
is wide (16:9, 2400 × 1350): the deck's name, "By" the player, then the date, format, deck count and sideboard count, with the Table 1 mark in the corner.

each card once with its count on the corner, creatures first, then spells, then lands. A line labelled Sideboard sets off the sideboard, shown as one overlapping column. Cards grow as large as the picture allows; very big decks make the picture taller instead.
instead lays the deck out in overlapping columns, one per group, each titled with its count.
Cards or Stacks; order by type, mana value, color or color identity; sideboard on or off; your name on or off (a friend's deck shows the owner's name). The preview updates as you change them.
Save to Photos (iPhone asks once, only to add photos; Android saves to Pictures › Table 1) or Share to Messages, Discord, Files and anything else, as a JPEG named for the deck.
Download the JPEG, Share it where the browser can, or Copy image to paste it anywhere. Your options are remembered.

tap the preview to open the picture full screen. Pinch (or scroll, on a computer) to zoom up to 8×, drag to look around, and double-tap (double-click) to jump to 3× and back. On the web, + and − zoom, 0 fits it again, and Esc closes the zoom. The top 100 (or 50) image of a cube ranking zooms the same way.

entries.t: Hold to copy, save or share
entries.x: a long press on the preview or the zoomed picture (the deck image and a ranking's top 100 image alike) offers Copy, Save to Photos and Share. On iPhone it's the phone's own menu with the picture above it (VoiceOver lists the three as actions); on the website it's the browser's own picture menu (hold on a phone, right-click with a mouse); on Android a Table 1 menu whose Copy puts the picture on the clipboard and whose Share shows it in the share sheet. Under the preview: "Tap to zoom · hold to copy, save or share".
Made on your device from the card file and card images; nothing is uploaded. Considering cards are left out.

Put a cube's cards in order, best first, the way cuberanker.com does for one famous cube, for any cube on Table 1. A ranking is one person's run through a cube, made of quick screens of up to four cards.

A Rankings row on every cube you can see: your own, or one a friend or someone you've played with shares on their profile. A cube shared with you by link gets it as soon as you follow it, on the link's own screen; it stays while the link is live and you follow.
lists your rankings across every cube, then Cubes you can rank, with each cube's owner, size and rankings. Rank <owner>'s cube starts your own.
A ranking of someone else's cube is wholly yours: they can see it (when it's shared with the cube) but never change it.

a ranking is titled with the name of the person who made it ("Mara Quinn"), everywhere it shows. An optional label follows the name ("Mara Quinn · Power only") to tell your rankings of one cube apart.

Sort each color (White, Blue, Black, Red, Green, Multicolor, Colorless, Lands): its Top 1/4, Top 1/3, Top half or Every card. Then the Final: a top 100 (or 50) across the whole cube. New rankings start at a quarter for a top 50 and a third for a top 100, until you pick.

The final always comes out exact, whatever the depth: when a color has more cards in your top 50 than it sorted, the final asks about them itself. A quarter takes about a third fewer screens than a half on a 540-card cube.
the final places a card only once its order against the other colors was asked directly (see Checks in the final, below), so one answer can't settle a whole run of cards.
Cards show in the printing the cube holds (a card with several printings shows the one it has most copies of).

Each screen shows up to four cards. Drag them into order (or tap two to swap), then Lock in. The app works out everything that follows, so it never asks the same thing twice, and says about how many screens are left.
Sometimes cards already in order show a lock, and only one card moves to find its place.
the last screen; on any card's history, Redo an earlier screen to answer it again. On the web, keys 1–4, the arrows, Enter and Z do it all.

Lists for the final and each color, then the cards "below the top N, in no particular order". Copy list copies it as text; Top 100 image makes a picture of it, which you can tap to zoom in on, or hold to copy, save or share.
Tap a card for its history and Why is it above…: the chain of screens that put one card over another.
Watch anyone's ranking live as they go.
/ranking puts your top 50, top 100 or one color's list in a Discord channel (see Discord).

From Insights → Limited (Rank this set, or New sets to rank) or Rankings (Sets you can rank: sets from the last year with 60 or more cards, sets due in the next 75 days once 20 of their cards are out, and every Arena cube run). The set's Rankings works like a cube's: Rank <set> starts yours, then sort each color and the final.
A set ranks its cards once each, English, no basic lands, tokens or art cards, each drawn in its regular frame. A cube run ranks the cards 17Lands lists for it.
Spoiler season works: cards the set gains after you start wait outside your lists until you place them, like a cube's new cards.
to start (or Only me): everyone can see a set, so your ranking goes to your friends rather than to everyone on Table 1. Your friends' rankings of the set are listed under yours, to watch and compare.

A tap opens the cube's Rankings: Rank PowerLSV starts yours (depth, top 50 or 100, Shared with friends or Only me), then Yours and Your friends'. Everything else is the cube ranker: colors, the final and its checks, first picks, compare with a brief, the Top 100 image, Discord's /ranking.
like a set ranking: your friends, and whoever your profile's Rankings setting reaches. It shows on your profile's Rankings with the others.

read from where each cube lives: Cube Cobra's lists (in the printings those cubes use), mtgo.com's current Vintage Cube list (Scryfall's copy is behind it), and Scryfall's Arena Powered Cube. They're read again every Monday; cards that join wait to be placed and cards that leave drop out, as with any cube. A source that can't be read, or reads under 300 cards, keeps the list as it was. Two of LSV's cards aren't in the card data and are left out.

Before the final places a card, it looks at each other color's best card still in. If no screen ever put your card's color and that color side by side, and the order came only from a third color between them, the next screen is a check: your card with those cards (and its own color's next card when only the color's sort put it above), nothing locked, read "Final · checking #31 of the top 50". An order that cards of two or more other colors already back up isn't checked.

Your answer on a check wins: if you now put Counterspell above Novice Inspector, the earlier answers that said otherwise give way. A check can also reorder two cards of one color the color's own sort got wrong.
The list keeps every place it already knows while the checks run; the final reads done once every place is checked. "About N to go" counts the places still to check.
A ranker who answers the same way every time gets the same list as before, after the checks.
Finished finals reopen for their checks.
Once the final is done, Open a pack: 15 cards from the cube. Pick the one you'd take first. The pick refines your ranking like any screen.

When your ranking already puts a card in the pack above your pick, it says so, for example "You ranked Mana Drain #3 and Fury #20, but picked Fury". Keep my ranking, or Let the pick win: the screens behind the disagreement come out and those cards are asked again.
lists every pick, the pack's best card by your ranking, and whether it disagreed.
Every place change is kept, newest first by day, and filterable by list: "Mana Drain · Final: #5 (new)", "Fury · Final: #4 → #9 (redo screen 12)". A card's history shows its own changes.
on any list: how many cards both have placed, how far apart they sit on average, the ten biggest differences, and the cards in one top half but not the other.

comes first: two to four short sentences written by Claude on where the two of you agree and the one or two clearest differences (colors, mana fixing, aggro or control, cheap interaction or big threats, the curve), naming a few cards. It knows which lands fix your mana and which are utility lands like Strip Mine or Karakas, and it gives each card's color as the card has it. It's written from both rankings' places, kept until either ranking changes, and refers to people only by name.

Cards that leave the cube drop out of your lists; what they told the ranking still counts, so your order stays. If one left your top 100 (or a color's top half), that list asks a screen or two to fill the place.
Cards that join wait under New in the cube, not placed yet, and the list keeps showing your order around them.

The ranking says what changed ("3 cards joined … and 2 cards left …"). Re-rank asks only about the new cards, mostly one new card against cards you've already ordered, then Next moves on to the next list that has one. Once every new card has a place, the note goes away.
When someone else starts a ranking of your cube that you can see, you get a notification (at most one a week per person). Tapping it opens their ranking on iPhone.
Each screen saves as you lock it in, one at a time. Undo and Redo take out only the screen you chose.

What isn't saved yet stays on your phone (or in your browser) through a crash, a force-quit, a closed tab or no signal, and is sent again until it's saved. A ranking with screens still to save says so, and tries again after a few seconds, then every minute.
If the ranking changed on another device, the app reads it again and adds your screens on top, rather than throwing them away.
A second tap on Lock in, or Enter pressed before the next screen draws, is ignored rather than locking the old order in again.
The server refuses any save that would take out screens you didn't take out, from any version of the app, and keeps every screen that leaves a ranking, so one can always be put back.

Your rankings show on your profile, under Rankings, to whoever your Rankings setting in Sharing reaches (Friends to start; see Sharing); a shared set ranking reaches those people too, not only your friends. A ranking starts Shared with the cube: everyone who can see the cube can see it, so a cube's owner sees every ranking of it. Switch to Only me in Settings, where you can also give it a Label (optional) or remove one, change its depth or size, or delete it. Labels others can see are checked like deck names.
Decks check every card against their format and call out problems at the top of the deck and on each card's row; Stats shows the same check for every other format.
What you see: "1 card isn't legal in Modern: Seething Song"; the row says Banned or Not legal. Formats: Standard, Pioneer, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Pauper, Commander, Premodern, Canadian Highlander.
What you see: "Restricted to 1" when a deck holds more than one copy across main and sideboard. Formats: Vintage.
What you see: "More than 4 copies", with exceptions for basics and cards like Relentless Rats. Formats: Standard, Pioneer, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Pauper, Premodern.
What you see: "Points: 7 of 10" with the pointed cards, turning red as "Over the points limit: 20 of 10"; each row shows its points. Formats: Canadian Highlander.
What you see: "Singleton" on a second copy of any non-basic card. Formats: Canadian Highlander, Commander.
What you see: "Canadian Highlander decks need at least 100 cards: 87 so far.". Formats: Canadian Highlander.

Legality comes from Scryfall and updates daily. Canadian Highlander points come from the official list at canadianhighlander.ca and refresh with every catalog update. Considering cards are flagged on their rows but don't make a deck illegal.
New deck → Find a deck online. Describe what you want ("latest Boros Energy from a big Modern event") and pick a format.

An AI agent (Claude) looks in Table 1's own results first: every Magic Online Challenge, Showcase, Qualifier and League decklist, and Melee.gg and TopDeck.gg paper events, read within the hour of being published, for Standard, Pioneer, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Pauper and Canadian Highlander (the same results Insights is built on). A list found there is copied exactly as published, with its event, date, finish and the page it came from. Then the web: mtgdecks.net, melee.gg, MTGGoldfish and official MTGO results, for Commander, Premodern, a paper event that isn't in, or a particular player's list.
lists from the last week, then 30 days, then 90. Among those it prefers strong finishes at large events (Pro Tour, Regional Championships, big opens, MTGO Challenges and Showcases).
If your request could mean different decks, it asks a short follow-up with suggested answers, and you can type your own.

You see the list with its event, date, placement, player and source link before creating the deck. Cards resolve to their original printings; any card it can't match is listed, never silently dropped.

entries.t: The search runs on the server
entries.x: tap Find deck and the phone is free. Lock it, switch apps or close the tab and the search goes on; a Deck found notification brings you back to the list when it's ready (a follow-up question comes as "Which deck?", a miss as "No list found"). While you stay on the screen it fills in by itself and no notification is shown.

under the searching notice, a Working list grows as the finder goes, the latest step marked "…": its own short remarks ("Let me check Table 1's results first."), "Checking Table 1's results: Modern, last 30 days, \"Energy\"", what it found there ("12 events with 190 decks, newest Modern Challenge 32 · 2026-10-31"), "Reading deck 169410 from Table 1's results" then "Read Boros Energy · 1st at Modern Challenge 32", "Searching the web: boros energy modern challenge" and "Reading www.mtgo.com/decklist/…". The steps stay with the search, so a search picked up again shows how it went. Open Find a deck again and a search still running, or finished in the last hour, is right there; on the website too, in a new tab. A search can take a minute or two; one that can't finish in four is called off and you're told.
Each account gets 20 searches a day; a second tap on the same search costs nothing.
New deck or New cube → Import from a link or list. Paste a link or the list itself, check the preview, rename it and pick the format, then create.

How it works: Paste the deck link.

makes the draft for you, gives from your for-trade binders and gets from theirs, ready in the trade editor.

Keep up with a friend's deck, cube or binder without checking it: follow it, and hear once they've finished a round of changes.
On any binder, deck or cube someone else shares with you (on their profile, or a link you opened), Follow sits above Export. Signed out on the website, it says to sign in.

Following, the row reads Following with a check; tap it to turn notifications off or on, or Unfollow. Under it, Changes shows the latest update ("+12 −8 · 2 h ago") and how many are new. What following brings shows at once, on the same screen.
following it also lets you rank it, and its Follow row says so ("…and rank it"). Rankings appears the moment you follow, and goes if you unfollow or the link stops.

You keep a follow only while you can see it. If the owner makes it private, stops the link you followed through, blocks you or deletes it, it reads "This isn't available" and sends nothing; if they share it again, it comes back. The owner is never told who follows, or how many.
Up to 500 follows.

Changes are gathered, not sent one by one: an update goes out once the list has had no changes for 30 minutes, and a list sends at most one update every 6 hours (later changes wait and join the next one).
An update is what changed overall since the last one: a card added and taken out again doesn't count, and a run of edits that ends where it began sends nothing.
Decks and cubes compare each card in each section (Main, Sideboard, Commander; Considering is left out); binders compare copies of each printing. Renaming doesn't count.
The notification names the list and says what came in and went out, with up to three card names. Turn one follow's notifications off and its updates still show in Following.
On the Collection tab, each followed deck, binder or cube sits on its row after your own, with its art (the owner's hero card, else its top card by copies), the owner's name and "N new".

The Following screen (from a follow notification, or the sidebar on a computer) lists each follow (updated first) with whose it is, its latest change and "N new". Tap to open it; More (or a long press) turns notifications off or unfollows.
lists each update since you followed, newest first, with Added and Taken out cards (in a deck, which section). Tap a card for its page. Updates from before you followed aren't shown.

Tapping it opens your trade match with them.

Wherever a person appears (profile, friend rows, requests, search results, trade matches) a long press or More offers Block and Report. Blocking hides your Library and profile from them and stops requests; they aren't told, and you can still both play the same event. A report picks a reason, takes an optional note, and can also block.

Only what other people can see is checked: names, handles, photos, shared deck, cube and binder names, event and guest names, shared deck photos. Private things are never sent anywhere. Claude judges each as allow, review or block, and knows that Murder, Thoughtseize and Death and Taxes are just Magic.

Content gets the least drastic, reversible fix (a name reset, a photo taken down, a deck name unshared); nobody is ever removed from an event. The owner gets a notice under Account → From Table 1 with one appeal. Restricting an account is always a person's decision.
Enforcement switches on after a week of verdicts has been checked.

The app asks for permission on the screen after sign-in that says what notifications are for, only when you tap Turn on. Skip it and the app doesn't ask again on its own; turn them on in iOS Settings.

(organizers): "Ana signed up · 12/16 players", "Bea joined the waitlist · 16/16 players · 3 waiting", "Cal dropped · 7/8 players", "Dee left the waitlist". Each new one replaces the last for that event, and a tap opens it. There's no switch to turn them off in the apps yet.
when a place opens in an event you're waiting for. A top 8 round's alert says "Quarterfinals is up", "Semifinals is up" or "The final is up".

Alerts arrive within seconds: invitations, a new round's pairing, results reported, disputed or changed, a cancelled event, a new event from an organizer you've played with in the last 90 days (never for private events), friend requests and accepts, and notices from Table 1.

a new format, set data, Arena cube run or set to rank, once each, for people who've opened Insights in the last 60 days. A tap opens Insights on it (or the set's Rankings). Off with the switch at the bottom of Insights → Limited; on Android it has its own group, New in Insights.
one a day at most, when wants got meaningfully cheaper or reached your max (see Binders and wants). Off with the Price alerts switch on Wants.

a deck finder search you started has finished ("Boros Energy · 1st · Modern Challenge 32 · 2026-10-30. Tap to create it.", "Which deck?", "No list found"). A tap opens Find a deck on that search; on Android it's in the Collection group.
a round of changes to a deck, cube or binder you follow, and a friend putting up cards you want, come as one alert each, not one per card. Tapping opens the Changes or the trade match.
Tapping an alert opens the event, Friends or Notices. Alerts older than 30 minutes are dropped rather than arriving late.

the same notifications with the same wording, in four groups you can turn off one by one in Android's settings: Events (pairings, results, invitations, sign-ups; shown at the top of the screen), Collection (follows, trade wants, price alerts, cube rankings), Friends and From Table 1. A newer one about the same thing replaces the older, and a tap opens the same screen as on iPhone; notices from Table 1 open From Table 1 and a moderator's review alert opens Review. The phone is signed up for notifications while you're signed in and taken off at sign-out.
The web has no notifications.
Your collection, binders, wants, decks, cubes and trades live in your account on the server and appear on every device you sign in to.

Each device keeps a copy so the Library opens instantly and works offline; changes show right away and are confirmed by the server. Cards you add (by hand or by scanning) show before the server answers, and come back off if the change fails.
Other devices pick up only what changed since they last checked, so syncing stays quick for large collections.
Repeated taps or retries never double-count: every change is applied exactly once.
Undo reverses a whole action (an add, a scan session, an import, a binder move, a trade) in one step.

reopening the app (after the screen slept, or from another app) brings you back to the same screen, mid-ranking included. On Android, after 30 minutes or more away it starts on Events again; the iPhone always keeps your place.
(Android): back from a card's page, a deck, cube, binder, All cards or a shared list opens where you left it, in any view, with opened printings and your search kept.
The web app loads the Library only when you open it, so players who just use events get a smaller, faster app.

the Events tab, every event you've opened (your match and the standings, or the organizer's round) and Insights keep their last answer on the device and open on it at once, then ask the server. When the server can't be reached, the screen keeps what it has and says Couldn't refresh · last updated 3 min ago (Events and Insights at the top, an event along the bottom); with nothing saved yet it shows the error with Try again.
an event refreshes when the app comes to the front (or the website's tab is shown again, or the browser says it's back online), and picks up live updates again.
a request with no answer after 25 seconds fails, so you see the saved screen or the error (uploads get two minutes).

entries.t: Cards you add offline are kept

a deck or cube you make, and every change to one (cards, format, a restore, a delete), is applied on the device and sent before the next sync, on iPhone, Android and the website; a deck not yet on your account says so at the top. once you've visited table-1.site, the site itself is kept by your browser, so it opens with no connection and every page shows what it has saved. A new version of the site takes over the next time you open it.

Sign in with Apple, Google, Discord or email. Any of them makes an account the first time. Android has no Apple button: Google, Discord or email there. An Apple account signs in on Android by email with the same address.

Continue with Discord opens Discord's own page (in a sheet on iPhone, a browser tab on Android, the same tab on the website), where you approve Table 1, then brings you back signed in. If your Discord email is verified and matches an existing Table 1 account, you sign in to that account; otherwise you get a new one. Closing the page or pressing Cancel on it simply takes you back.

in the apps, Google's own sign-in sheet; on the website, Continue with Google goes straight to Google, which says "to continue to table-1.site" (and will name Table 1 once Google has verified the brand), then brings you back to the page you were on. Cancel at Google and you're back there, signed out.

Enter your address and you get one email from Table 1 with both a Sign in button and a one-time code. Type the code on any device, or tap the button: with the app installed it opens the app and signs you in; on a computer it signs you in on the website.

A sign-in email can go to an address once a minute. Ask again sooner and you go straight to the code step, with Resend counting down to when you can ask again, because the email is already on its way. If too many sign-in emails have gone out from Table 1 in the last hour, it says "Too many sign-in emails right now. Wait a few minutes, or continue with Apple or Google." (on Android: "with Google or Discord") A double tap (or Return as well as Send) sends one email.

entries.t: The code step waits for you
entries.x: after an email is sent, leave for your mail app and come back (even if your phone closed the app, or you reloaded the page) and you're on the code step for that address, for the code's hour. Change email, signing in, or the hour passing clears it. Not there? Check spam.

A new email or Discord account asks for your first and last name before anything else, so organizers and opponents see a real name (Discord only shares your username). Apple and Google accounts skip this.

at the top looks through every answer and the guide at once, from two letters. Results come best match first, each saying where it's from ("FAQ · Running events", "Guide · Card scanning"). Table 1 as a bot in your Discord server: make events, sign up and drop with a button, see who's in, and post the results with a link to the event, all from the channel. The bot acts as each person's own Table 1 account, with the same rules as the apps.
Anyone with Manage Server adds it from table-1.site/discord (Add to your server). It asks only to send messages and embed links; it never reads anyone's messages.

once: the bot answers you, and only you, with a link that works for 10 minutes. Open it, sign in to Table 1 (Apple, Google, email or Discord; it makes the account if you're new) and you're linked. If you sign in to Table 1 with Discord anyway, you're linked already and can skip this. /unlink undoes it, as does Account → Discord on the website.
(Manage Server) sets the zone the server's event times are typed in; everyone sees posted times in their own.

pick the format (Standard to Canadian Highlander, Other, Draft or Sealed), and if you like a name, when ("2026-11-07 18:30"), where, a player cap, top 8, the number of rounds (left out, it follows the sign-ups), a set code or a cube. For a draft, pods and pairing (Inside pods or Across pods), as in the app. You're seated as the organizer, and the event is a real Table 1 event you also run from the app.

the bot posts shows the name, format, when (in each reader's own time zone) and where, the organizer, the players by name with "3/8", the waitlist, rounds, top cut and the join code, with Sign up and Open in Table 1; a draft with more than one pod adds a Pods line (the split before the draw, the pods as seated after). It redraws itself whenever the event changes, from anywhere: a sign-up or drop in the app, on the website, through the link or here; the waitlist moving up; the organizer's changes to players, cap, name, time or venue; each round; the finish. Once round 1 is paired only the link stays. If someone deletes the card, the bot stops updating it; /event post puts up a new one.

seats you (or puts you on the waitlist when the event is full: "You're number 2 on the waitlist"). Already in? The bot tells you so, privately, with a Drop button. puts the card of an event you made in the app in the channel: pick it from your own events (the ones you run or play in, open ones first) or paste its link. A player can post an event they're in unless it's private. /event list shows the server's open events; /event show shows one card just to you.

posts the final standings (rank, name, record and points, the winner with a trophy, the top 8 in full) with a link to the standings on Table 1. The picker offers the server's events and your own (run or played in), finished first, so an event run from the app can have its results posted here; it joins the server as they're posted. Before the event ends, the organizer can post standings so far. A draft with two or more pods puts each player's pod beside their name ("1. Ana · P1 · 3-0 · 9 pts"). Team events (team draft, team sealed) show each team on its own instead, with its record, points and match wins, and its players under it best first with their records.

posts one of your decks: name, format, card counts, its Spice, the whole deck as a picture (the deck image's cards layout, drawn on the server) and Open on Table 1. The link is the same "Anyone with the link" as in Sharing, so the bot asks before it makes one, and you can stop sharing it there any time.

and /trades post your wants or your cards for trade: the whole list (25 lines, then "and N more"), or one card picked as you type. Each line has the printing (or "any printing"), the finish, the condition for trade, and the price: the cheapest near-mint price a want takes, or a for-trade copy's price at its condition, with the list's value at market. Open on Table 1 opens the part's link; the bot asks before it makes one. Your max prices never show.
looks a card up: cost, type, cheapest TCGplayer price (and foil), how many printings, the card's picture.

posts Insights as a picture: matchups (the grid: every archetype with 1% of the decks against the 10 most played, each square's win rate and record, faded under 30 matches; each row's name carries its overall win rate and record, tinted like a square ), deck (one archetype, picked as you type, against each other: bars with the record and a 95% likely range, the matchups with 30+ matches first) or winrates (every archetype with 20+ matches: record, win rate and 95% range, best first, Other last; teal when the whole range is above 50%, pink when below). Choose the format (Standard, Pioneer, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Pauper or Canadian Highlander), All or Big events, and 7, 14, 30 or 90 days (All events and 30 days when left out). The post links to the same view in Table 1. Anyone can use it, linked or not.

posts one of your cube or set rankings: pick it as you type from the ones you made ("Lindmark Cube · Summer · 50/50 ranked"; sets with their code), and show its Top 50, Top 100 or one color's list (left out, its own top 50 or 100). Open in Table 1 shows only when the ranking is shared. Only your own rankings, and posting one changes nothing on Table 1. The places come out exactly as the app shows them.
lists every command, just for you.
